request.input: From your answer, I'll assume I should establish non-negotiable boundaries with my sister to keep our relationship sustainable. Right?

content.text:
**Yes, that is exactly correct.**

It may feel counterintuitive—or even "mean"—to set firm boundaries with someone who has suffered as much as your sister has. However, in the context of BPD and trauma, boundaries are actually an act of love.

Here is why boundaries are the primary tool for sustainability in your specific situation:

**1. Boundaries prevent "Caregiver Burnout"**
If you allow the manipulation and financial instability to bleed into your own life, you will eventually hit a wall of resentment and exhaustion. Once you burn out, you will either snap at her or collapse yourself, and then you will be unable to provide any support at all. Boundaries protect your capacity to love her.

**2. Boundaries provide a "Predictable World"**
People with BPD often grew up in chaotic environments (like the one you described with your mother) where rules were inconsistent or nonexistent. While she may fight your boundaries at first, having a consistent, predictable set of "rules" for how you will and will not be treated actually provides a sense of stability that she likely never had as a child.

**3. Boundaries stop the "Enabling Cycle"**
If her past marriages ended in disaster and she racked up massive debt, it suggests a pattern of impulsivity. If you step in to "fix" the consequences of those impulses, she has no external incentive to engage in the hard work of therapy (like DBT). Boundaries move the responsibility for her life back onto her.

**A final tip on implementation:**
When you establish these boundaries, do it during a **"Cold State"** (when things are calm and you are both getting along), not during a **"Hot State"** (in the middle of an argument). 

Say something like: *"I love you so much and I want us to live together happily for a long time. To make sure that happens, I need to set some ground rules for myself regarding [money/communication/respect]. This is how I'm going to handle things moving forward so that I can stay healthy and keep being there for you."*
